newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cotti blames both sides for Nazi-Swiss debacle.
newsitem.headline: Cotti blames both sides for Nazi-Swiss debacle.

text.p: Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, in remarks published on Sunday, blamed both the Swiss and the United States for bad blood which has put the countries at loggerheads over missing assets of Jewish Nazi victims.

In an interview with the Swiss Sunday newspaper "SonntagsZeitung", Cotti said the Swiss were partly to blame for dragging their feet but urged Washington to allow time for thorough investigation of the matter.
At the same time he rejected allegations by New York Republican Senator Alfonse D'Amato that the Swiss were purposely blocking an investigation.

D'Amato, who heads the powerful Senate Banking Committee, is leading an investigation into Swiss banks' wartime activities. He is seeking renegotiation of the 1946 Washington Agreement in which the Swiss agreed to pay 250 million Swiss francs in compensation for wartime purchases of gold which Nazis amassed from countries they took over, or stole outright from Jews and other victims.

D'Amato, in an interview with the Swiss newspaper Journal de Geneve earlier this month, asked: "How can one have confidence in the Swiss authorities when they have only taken action under pressure from public opinion?"
He also said that the five-year period a Swiss commission has sought to look into disappeared bank accounts is too long.

"Whether his (D'Amato's) assertions are correct with respect to Switzerland and Swiss banks during and after the Nazi period must be cleared up by the historians," said Cotti in the SonntagsZeitung interview.

"We want a complete clarification of all open questions. But in any case, this requires some time. His accusations, however, that we would delay the investigations, or that we were not credible, because we are Swiss, are insulting and absolutely unacceptable. I reject them in all forms," Cotti said.

"I do not know what motives D'Amato has. Certainly, however, the whole theme of assets of Nazi victims has been a topic which has been mentioned very little over a very long time. Only in the last few months has one really become aware that this tragic era has not really been dealt with. Mr. D'Amato has, in addition, also only recently begun his offensive," Cotti added.
Switzerland appointed Thomas Borer, an international lawyer, on Friday to head a task force which is to coordinate inquiries into what happened to Nazi victims' assets.

The Swiss government has ordered banks to waive their tough secrecy laws and help with the investigation. In May, the banks too, after some delay, agreed to work with international Jewish organisations on the matter of stolen assets.

"The subject was for a long time -- not just in Switzerland -- hardly visible (discussed). At the start of May, the Bankers' Association and the various international Jewish Organisations decided to set up an independent committee to clear up the matter of looking into Swiss banks' (holdings of unclaimed assets after the war)," Cotti said.

"Also in May, the Swiss Parliament emphasised that it was prepared to discuss the question of whether Swiss financial institutions took in stolen assets from Nazi victims. In the process, a Federal ruling was...passed unanimously by the larger house... So, it wasn't as if nothing was done," he added.
After the House ruling, the Swiss Senate is expected to grant final approval in December to a group of experts to investigate the matter.
However, Cotti admitted that the Swiss have been slow to respond, at least with respect to latest recent allegations.

These include latest reports that Switzerland may have acted illegally according to a 1949 agreement, whereby assets held by Swiss banks which belonged to Polish Nazi victims were handed over to the Polish government, as part of an agreement to gain compensation for Swiss citizens who lost assets in Poland when the Communist government took over there.
"Indeed, we have been overtaken by the events in the last few days," Cotti said. He urged that the Swiss experts looking into the matter be given sufficient time.
"They must take up their job in December... But then we must give them the time which they need to make a serious and complete clarification," he said.
